newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals-Copper in Singapore, rally to persist.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals-Copper in Singapore, rally to persist.

text.p: Some 20,000 tonnes of copper is said to be in Singapore, but those holding the material have refrained from placing the copper on warrant, Singapore metal traders said on Friday.

"It would be in their interest to create an impression of a shortage in copper so they can sell it at a higher price later," a senior dealer at a Western metal trading company told Reuters. "That's the only reason I can think of why they have not placed it on warrant."

Vinod Kumar, director of Singapore-based metal company Donald Mcarthy, estimated the material already in Singapore at only 4,000 tonnes while other dealers said the amount ranges from 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes.
"It's not being placed on warrant," Kumar said, adding there is no compelling reason for the material to be put there anyway. "I will never put it (on warrant)."
"The downside of this is they won't receive the backwardation by leaving it in the market," another dealer said.

Base metal prices are expected to extend their rally in the London Metal Exchange (LME) even though copper and aluminium appear to be vulnerable to bouts of profit-taking and producer-selling, traders said.
"$1,980 was a big resistance level. Now, it (copper) could go up to US$2,100 (a tonne)," Kumar said.
"If the shorts panic and start some shortcovering, copper could lift itself above $2,050," one trader added.
One dealer said "there may be some early profit-taking and selling, but the stocks report should stop that."
Singapore-based metal dealers said copper stocks may fall by 10,000-15,000 tonnes while aluminium stocks should slide by about 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes when the LME report comes out at 0900 GMT.
One trader said, though, that aluminium may rise or fall by only 1,000 tonnes in the LME report.
"It (copper) should go down by about 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes," one trader said. "That seems to be the consensus here although it's really confusing where the material is going."
Another drawdown should give a fillip to base metal prices, but dealers here doubt if the rally can be sustained.

"The rally will fizzle out and the market will come back to $1,900 (a tonne)," Kumar said. "Fundamentals do not support prices going up. The demand for copper is not there. Speculators are playing the game."
"I don't think the market is acting along fundamental lines," one trader conceded. "This is just a technical rally."
A dealer for a Japanese metal trading firm said the surge in LME should eventually lose steam once selling hits the market over the next week or so.
"I think copper should go back to around $1,970 a tonne. This rally has been a bit overdone," the dealer said.
Three month copper was being quoted in Singapore at around $2,013/18 a tonne at 0330 GMT, little changed from the late trade in London on Thursday of $2,017.
Aluminium was being quoted at the same time at about $1,468/73 a tonne, slightly up from London's late trade yesterday of $1,466.50, which is a two-month high.
Premiums in the city-state eased slightly on weak demand, metal traders said.
Copper premiums were being quoted at around $100 a tonne, against $100-$120 last week while aluminium was slightly easier at $80-$85 a tonne from $85.
"There's not just a great deal of business going and I haven't heard of any trading for some time," a dealer said.
